governing_question: After everything we have seen, what kind of political-economic system is this—and what is it not?
central_line: Constitutional Capitalism is not capitalism weakened by constitutional limits. It is capitalism made more durable by constitutional limits.
canonical_definition_long: Constitutional Capitalism is a market-based political-economic system that protects individual liberty, broadens the ability of households and communities to build capital, keeps economic and political power from capturing one another, uses government only within defined constitutional roles, and measures success by whether prosperity and productive capability compound across generations.
canonical_definition_short: Free people. Competitive markets. Distributed power. Broader ownership. Capable communities. Prosperity that compounds.
countable_meaning: We have not yet proven alternative public cash sufficient to spend or use for tax replacement.

seven_commitments.title: The household is the unit of success
seven_commitments.body: Not GDP alone. Not government revenue. Not the stock market. Ask whether households retain more, own more, become less fragile, gain agency, and control more of their time.

seven_commitments.title: Markets are the primary discovery system
seven_commitments.body: Prices, competition, risk, profit, and experimentation matter. But markets must remain genuinely contestable.

seven_commitments.title: Ownership matters
seven_commitments.body: Who owns productive assets affects where long-term wealth accumulates. Ownership should be broadened where practical, not imposed ideologically.

seven_commitments.title: Government must be capable and bounded
seven_commitments.body: Weak government is not limited government. Capable government is necessary. Unbounded government is dangerous.

seven_commitments.title: Public participation in upside must be earned
seven_commitments.body: If the public meaningfully contributes capital or bears risk, a defensible public claim may exist. But no revenue is counted until the waterfall proves it.

seven_commitments.title: Economic and political power must not fuse
seven_commitments.body: Private success is legitimate. Buying the rules is not. Government authority is legitimate. Owning the economy through political authority is not.

seven_commitments.title: Prosperity should compound across generations
seven_commitments.body: A generation should not look prosperous by consuming the infrastructure, institutions, natural capital, or fiscal capacity of the next.

what_it_is_not.title: Not laissez-faire
what_it_is_not.body: Markets can fail. Monopoly can form. Costs can be pushed onto others. Economic power can become political power. Government has a legitimate role in protecting market conditions and public rights.

what_it_is_not.title: Not socialism
what_it_is_not.body: Private productive property is not presumed illegitimate. Private enterprise is not a temporary compromise. Profit is not something the system seeks to abolish.

what_it_is_not.title: Not state capitalism
what_it_is_not.body: Government does not own important industries merely because they are important. Public ownership is narrow and must pass the eight-gate standard.

what_it_is_not.title: Not social democracy
what_it_is_not.body: Social democracy often accepts private-market production, then uses taxation and public services to redistribute or insure against outcomes. Constitutional Capitalism also asks an earlier question: Who owns productive assets and who receives the returns before redistribution? That does not make redistribution disappear. It changes what we pay attention to.

what_it_is_not.title: Not libertarianism
what_it_is_not.body: CC does not assume all legitimate collective problems can be solved through voluntary private action alone. It accepts public goods, market failures, constitutional public authority, and limited public investment where justified.

what_it_is_not.title: Not communism
what_it_is_not.body: Private ownership, profit, markets, entrepreneurship, and differentiated outcomes remain fundamental.

what_it_is_not.title: Not protectionism
what_it_is_not.body: Arkansas should trade. Arkansas should import things other places make better. Net-capability retention is not buy-local nationalism.

what_it_is_not.title: Not technocracy
what_it_is_not.body: Experts matter. Data matters. AI may help. But expertise never becomes sovereignty.

what_it_is_not.title: Not equality of outcome
what_it_is_not.body: People will make different choices, take different risks, and end up with different wealth. The system's concern is liberty, capability, fair rules, competitive markets, broad opportunity, and resistance to capture — not identical outcomes.

sections.heading: You have already seen it
prose: You already know most of the answer. You have seen the household as the unit of success; money as a flow that can build or fail to build capital; people as the core productive asset; essential systems as interdependent; markets as powerful but vulnerable to concentration; government as necessary but dangerous when unconstrained; public investment as narrow, conditional, and evidence-gated; power as something that must circulate back to the people.
Constitutional Capitalism is the name we give to the system that joins those pieces together.
Not a brand first. A synthesis first.

sections.heading: Start with the two words
prose: Constitutional means: rights before convenience; delegated power, not surrendered sovereignty; no blank check for majorities; no blank check for government; no blank check for private wealth to buy the rules; institutional limits strong enough to survive bad leadership.

Capitalism means: private ownership remains legitimate; markets remain central; profit remains legitimate; entrepreneurship remains valuable; investment remains necessary; price signals matter; decentralized economic decision-making remains the default.
Constitutional Capitalism is not capitalism weakened by constitutional limits. It is capitalism made more durable by constitutional limits.

sections.heading: What it is not
prose: This is one of the strongest sections in the public book — because misunderstanding CC usually begins by confusing it with a neighbor.

Not laissez-faire: Markets can fail. Monopoly can form. Costs can be pushed onto others. Economic power can become political power. Government has a legitimate role in protecting market conditions and public rights.
Not socialism: Private productive property is not presumed illegitimate. Private enterprise is not a temporary compromise. Profit is not something the system seeks to abolish.
Not state capitalism: Government does not own important industries merely because they are important. Public ownership is narrow and must pass the eight-gate standard.

Not social democracy: Social democracy often accepts private-market production, then uses taxation and public services to redistribute or insure against outcomes. Constitutional Capitalism also asks an earlier question: Who owns productive assets and who receives the returns before redistribution? That does not make redistribution disappear. It changes what we pay attention to.

Not libertarianism: CC does not assume all legitimate collective problems can be solved through voluntary private action alone. It accepts public goods, market failures, constitutional public authority, and limited public investment where justified.
Not communism: Private ownership, profit, markets, entrepreneurship, and differentiated outcomes remain fundamental.
Not protectionism: Arkansas should trade. Arkansas should import things other places make better. Net-capability retention is not buy-local nationalism.
Not technocracy: Experts matter. Data matters. AI may help. But expertise never becomes sovereignty.

Not equality of outcome: People will make different choices, take different risks, and end up with different wealth. The system's concern is liberty, capability, fair rules, competitive markets, broad opportunity, and resistance to capture — not identical outcomes.

sections.heading: The seven core commitments
prose: 1. The household is the unit of success — Not GDP alone. Not government revenue. Not the stock market. Ask whether households retain more, own more, become less fragile, gain agency, and control more of their time.
2. Markets are the primary discovery system — Prices, competition, risk, profit, and experimentation matter. But markets must remain genuinely contestable.
3. Ownership matters — Who owns productive assets affects where long-term wealth accumulates. Ownership should be broadened where practical, not imposed ideologically.
4. Government must be capable and bounded — Weak government is not limited government. Capable government is necessary. Unbounded government is dangerous.

5. Public participation in upside must be earned — If the public meaningfully contributes capital or bears risk, a defensible public claim may exist. But no revenue is counted until the waterfall proves it.
6. Economic and political power must not fuse — Private success is legitimate. Buying the rules is not. Government authority is legitimate. Owning the economy through political authority is not.
7. Prosperity should compound across generations — A generation should not look prosperous by consuming the infrastructure, institutions, natural capital, or fiscal capacity of the next.

sections.heading: The two domination problems
prose: Constitutional Capitalism fears two forms of domination.
State domination: government becomes too powerful to challenge.
Private domination: economic power becomes concentrated enough to dominate markets, workers, communities, or government itself.
The purpose is not to eliminate power. It is to keep power divided, contestable, visible, and accountable.

sections.heading: The freedom triangle
prose: Political freedom: Can you speak, vote, organize, challenge government, and retain rights?
Economic freedom: Can you work, own, contract, invest, build, trade, and create?
Practical agency: Do you actually have enough capability, security, access, and time to exercise those freedoms meaningfully?

Political freedom without practical agency can become hollow. Economic freedom without competition can become domination. Material security without constitutional liberty can become dependency on power. CC tries to hold all three together.

sections.heading: Why “constitutional” comes first
prose: Imagine Arkansas discovers a brilliant economic model that increases average prosperity by 30%. But it requires suppressing political opposition, eliminating due process, seizing private property arbitrarily, assigning occupations, restricting movement, or letting AI make unappealable state decisions.
CC rejects it.
Prosperity is a means to human flourishing under liberty. It is not a license to override liberty.
That's why Constitutional comes first.

sections.heading: Why “capitalism” stays in the name
prose: Markets and private capital are not temporary devices CC tolerates. They are central because information is decentralized; people possess different knowledge; experimentation matters; profit can reward useful risk; loss can reveal failure; competition can discipline producers; entrepreneurship can create things government never predicted.
The state cannot know enough to plan a prosperous society from the center.
But markets cannot guarantee on their own that economic power will remain competitive or politically neutral.
That's the tension CC is designed around.

sections.heading: Compare the traditions directly
prose: The public book explains the distinction. The Comparison Explorer teaches the intellectual history. The Unabridged proves the technical architecture.
PUBLIC BOOK → UNDERSTAND. EXPLORER → LEARN. UNABRIDGED → PROVE.
Use the matrix below, then go deeper in the Explorer — not by stuffing thirty pages of philosophy history into this chapter.

sections.heading: Where CC borrows
prose: Constitutional Capitalism borrows or learns from: classical liberalism (rights, property, limits); market capitalism (decentralized exchange, profit, entrepreneurship); ordoliberal/social-market thought (markets require rules that preserve competition); social democracy (insecurity and essential systems matter); distributist/cooperative traditions (broad ownership matters); public-choice theory (government actors respond to incentives); federalism/subsidiarity (scale matters); resilience theory (efficiency alone is insufficient); intergenerational public-finance thinking (today's decisions affect future capacity).
The claim is not that every component is new. The claim is that the architecture joining them is the project.

sections.heading: Where CC rejects each tradition
prose: From laissez-faire: reject market outcomes as sufficient evidence of legitimacy.
From socialism: reject broad socialization of productive ownership as the default solution.
From social democracy: reject redistribution after production as the full answer to ownership concentration.
From state capitalism: reject political direction of commercial winners.
From libertarianism: reject the assumption that voluntary markets alone can solve every public good, externality, and infrastructure problem.
From technocracy: reject expertise as a substitute for popular sovereignty.
From populism: reject majoritarian will as sufficient to override rights or evidence.

sections.heading: The eight questions CC asks everywhere
prose: For any policy, business relationship, public program, or market:
1. Who owns it?
2. Who decides?
3. Who pays?
4. Who benefits?
5. Who bears the risk?
6. Where does the surplus go?
7. What happens to the household?
8. What happens when it fails?
These eight questions turn the philosophy into something people can use themselves.

sections.heading: Same problem, different systems
prose: A rural hospital is closing.
Laissez-faire: if the market cannot sustain it, resources may need to reallocate.
Social democracy: universal access may justify subsidy or public support.
Democratic socialism: healthcare infrastructure may be socially or publicly provided more broadly.
State capitalism: government may direct or own strategic capacity.

Constitutional Capitalism first asks: Is emergency healthcare an essential public function? Is the market thin? Is capacity regionally available? Can private provision be preserved? What is the narrowest intervention? Who bears risk? What outcome must be measured? What is the failure exit?

sections.heading: Same billionaire, different question
prose: Suppose an Arkansan invents something useful and becomes worth $10 billion. Does CC consider that a failure? No.
Then suppose that person uses wealth to purchase competitors, prevent market entry, obtain special legislation, direct public contracts, or capture regulators.
Now the problem isn't the number $10 billion. It's how economic power is being converted into structural domination.

sections.heading: Same government, different question
prose: Suppose Arkansas owns an energy asset earning money. CC does not automatically celebrate it.

Ask: Was public ownership necessary? Was there legal authority? Did public capital add something private capital would not? Is competition neutral? Is risk bounded? Is performance independently measured? Can it fail? Is it insulated from political capture?
Eight gates. The word “public” is not a moral certificate.

sections.heading: What Stage 4 changed
prose: The philosophy was not protected from evidence. Tell the reader what died.

Near-term dual tax abolition — failed. Public ownership as default — failed. Buy-local as a moral rule — failed. Credit equals prosperity — failed. Worker ownership always helps — failed. Demand-side housing without supply — failed. Retraining solves AI displacement — failed. Responsible leaders are enough — failed.
Constitutional Capitalism is the version that survived being attacked—not the version we started with.

sections.heading: What remains unproven
prose: Public-income opportunities remain unproven as COUNTABLE cash. Some legal edges remain uncertain. Some behavioral responses require pilots. Geographic Money Statements need deeper data. AI transition outcomes remain uncertain. Public investment must be judged case by case. Some resilience thresholds remain to be calibrated in implementation.
COUNTABLE = $0.
Meaning: We have not yet proven alternative public cash sufficient to spend or use for tax replacement.

sections.heading: What would make CC stop being CC?
prose: A policy is not Constitutional Capitalism if it: violates constitutional rights for economic gain; removes competitive markets without strong functional justification; gives government unlimited commercial power; treats private ownership as inherently suspect; assumes local is always better; counts hypothetical public money; relies on hidden algorithms exercising state power; grants political allies powers we would fear in opponents; shields failed programs from correction; treats people as economic inputs rather than rights-bearing individuals; substitutes expert rule for citizen sovereignty.
That's the semantic-capture lock in public language.

sections.heading: The one-sentence definition
prose: Only now — after the pieces — the canonical definition:

Constitutional Capitalism is a market-based political-economic system that protects individual liberty, broadens the ability of households and communities to build capital, keeps economic and political power from capturing one another, uses government only within defined constitutional roles, and measures success by whether prosperity and productive capability compound across generations.
Shorthand:
Free people. Competitive markets. Distributed power. Broader ownership. Capable communities. Prosperity that compounds.

sections.heading: What it looks like in ordinary life
prose: Return to the Rivers family. CC does not promise a government check for everything, government ownership of their employer, fixed prices, guaranteed wealth, or protection from every failure.

It aims for a system where work produces meaningful opportunity; essential systems do not constantly consume every gain; markets remain competitive; ownership is reachable; government is visible and challengeable; public money is traceable; shocks do not destroy everything built; and children inherit greater capability.

sections.heading: Not left, not right, but accountable to the test
prose: Avoid claiming transcendence from politics. The system will sometimes produce conclusions people associate with the right. Other times with the left. Sometimes neither.
The test isn't ideological origin. It is: constitutional? evidence-supported? market-compatible where markets function? anti-capture? household-positive? resilient? reversible/correctable if wrong?
The philosophy is not a promise that we already know every answer. It is a discipline for deciding which answers deserve to survive.
Next: Building the Bridge — how Arkansas gets from the state that exists now to a system that can be proven, not merely declared.
